1:
The chapter opens Job's reply to Eliphaz, and before a single complaint is uttered the witnesses pause over the temper of the whole debate. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry observes that both Job and his friends took the way disputants commonly take, undervaluing one another's sense and wisdom and management; the longer the saw of contention is drawn the hotter it grows, and the beginning of such strife is as the letting forth of water, so that it were better left off before it be meddled with. Eliphaz had branded Job's discourses as idle and unprofitable and nothing to the purpose, and Job, Henry says, now gives his the same character; those who are free in passing such censures must expect to have them retorted, for it is easy, it is endless, but cui bono? — angry answers stir up men's passions but never convince their judgments nor set truth in a clear light.

The latin-fathers Gregory the Great reads the reply against a larger backdrop, finding it a peculiar way with the wicked to urge their own bad points slanderously against the good before they are themselves accused, and, dreading reproach for the things they do, to testify that the righteous who withstand them commit the same. Holy men, he says, hear with forbearance even what they never remember to have done; and so blessed Job, seeing Eliphaz break out of words of comfort into the bitterness of upbraiding and show himself a feigned comforter, by his own patience maintains a type of the Church, which is wont to endure such things, and, when her cause is heard, to bring the calumnies to nothing by reasoning.

The reformed John Gill marks only the plain occasion — as soon as Eliphaz had done speaking, Job stood up and made his reply — while the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sketches the movement of the whole speech: Job, finding the argument useless, ceases to continue it, and after complaining of the way his friends have conducted it, and contrasting their treatment of him with the treatment he would give them were they in his case, he enlarges again upon his condition and makes a touching appeal to heaven, ending with the declaration that his case is desperate. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the same shape as an argument: Job replies to Eliphaz, and through him to all his friends, who instead of comforting him had added to his misfortunes; he shows how differently he would have used them, details his sufferings, and consoles himself with the consciousness of his own innocence, of which he takes God to witness. The witnesses do not divide; together they frame a reply that is at once a rebuke of false comfort and the opening of a fresh appeal from men to God.
2:
Job's first word to Eliphaz is a weary verdict on the whole procession of speeches, that he has heard many such things and his comforters are miserable comforters all. The reformed John Gill keeps the complaint concrete: Job had heard such maxims about the punishment of the wicked reported many times from his teachers and his parents, as Eliphaz had from his, so that there was nothing new, but crambe millies cocta, the same cold dish served over and over; he gave it the hearing, and scarcely that, it being altogether inapplicable to him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the very word: one has now heard rabboth, much, amply sufficient of this kind of speech, which is meant to comfort but primarily accuses and wounds instead of soothing; the friends are altogether consolatores onerosi, troublesome comforters who, instead of alleviating, only cause amal, molestiam.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the reproach home. Adam Clarke hears Job say the sayings of the ancients are not strange to him but do not apply to his case: they see him in affliction and should endeavour to console him, and yet, pretending to do it, prove miserable comforters all. John Wesley reduces it to a single point — these things are but vulgar and trivial, and so, he adds, are all creatures to a soul under deep conviction of sin or the arrest of death.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the two faults Job charges. There is the needless repetition, 'you tell me nothing but what I knew before, nothing but what you yourselves have said, it is the same thing over and over again,' which Henry owns is provoking and nauseous from an adversary, though from a teacher precept upon precept is often necessary and must not be grievous to the learner. And there is the unskilful application: they came to comfort him but went about it awkwardly, and, touching his case, quite mistook it, so that instead of alleviating the affliction they added to it. What Job says here, Henry insists, is true of all creatures in comparison with God; one time or other we shall be made to see and own that miserable comforters are they all, for under convictions of sin, terrors of conscience, and the arrests of death, it is only the blessed Spirit that can comfort effectually, and all others without him do it miserably, singing songs to a heavy heart to no purpose. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the sting of a phrase, that the friends' words are trite rather than true, or at least not the whole truth: 'common is the common-place, and vacant chaff well meant for grain.' The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the bitterest of Job's present griefs is the cold comfort of friends who repeat what he knows and miss what he feels.
3:
Turning Eliphaz's own charge back upon him, Job asks whether vain words shall have an end, and what it is that emboldens his friend to answer. The reformed John Gill notes that 'words of wind' is the very reproach Eliphaz had insinuated against Job at ch. 15:2, and Job retorts it: such worthless discourses, great swelling bubbles that look big and have nothing in them, should have a speedy end, and it were wiser to be silent than to speak to no better purpose. To carry them on at length, he suggests, is only to weary the hearer with emptiness, and it would be no small piece of wisdom in the friends to see that they had said enough and to break off.

The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen the second clause into a thrust at Eliphaz's competence. Adam Clarke renders 'vain words' literally as 'words of air,' and reads 'what emboldeneth thee' as a challenge — 'thou art totally ignorant of the business; what then can induce thee to take part in this discussion?' John Wesley hears plain impatience, 'when wilt thou put an end to these impertinent discourses?', and marks that Job here flings back upon Eliphaz the very charge Eliphaz had made against him at ch. 15:2-3, where the friend had accused Job of filling his belly with the east wind.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the idiom, judging that the English sense rather requires, 'shall not vain words have an end? for if not, what emboldeneth or provoketh thee that thou answerest?' The point of the question, on his reading, is that Eliphaz had contributed nothing to the discussion in his last reply but had simply reiterated what had been said before, so that his boldness in answering is a boldness with no fresh matter behind it. Here the movement of the argument shows plainly: what began as counsel has hardened into mere repetition, each side charging the other with wind, and Job, hearing nothing new, demands to know what gives his friend the confidence to keep speaking when he has nothing to add. The witnesses converge on the same reading of the verse — that Job is not merely venting irritation but exposing the emptiness of a rebuke that has run out of substance, and pressing his comforters to the silence that alone could now become them. It is the retort of a man who feels that the debate has become a contest of who can say the same thing longest, and who would gladly see it ended.
4:
Job now bids his friends change places with him in imagination, and asks how their fine speeches would sound then. The reformed John Gill reads the opening as scornful concession — 'I also could speak as ye do,' with as big words and as high a tone, were our conditions reversed; or, taken as a question, 'ought I to speak as you do?' which conscience would never suffer him to do. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the cutting reproof and calls it very affecting. Job desires his friends, for a little while, to change conditions with him, to put their souls in his soul's stead and suppose themselves in misery like him and him at ease like them — no absurd or foreign supposition, Henry adds, but one that the sudden vicissitudes of human affairs might quickly make true in fact, for the spokes of the wheel soon change places, and whatever our brethren's sorrows are, we ought by sympathy to make them our own, because we know not how soon they may be so.

Then, Henry says, Job represents the unkindness of their conduct by showing what he could do to them if they were down and he at ease: 'I could heap up words against you, as you do against me, and shake my head at you; and how would you like it? how would you bear it?' It is an easy thing, Henry observes, to trample upon those that are down and to find fault with what men say in the extremity of pain.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke prefers to render the potential verbs in the plain future, 'I also will speak,' and unfolds the menace of the head-shaking: were the friends in his place, he could quote many wise sayings tending to prove them hypocrites and wicked men, and, not choosing to say all, could shake his head by way of dark insinuation that much more lay behind — 'but would this be right?' That such sayings are in the memory, Clarke notes, is no proof that they were made for him or apply to his case. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott leaves it doubtful whether this verse stands in contrast to the kindness of v.5 or in parallel with it, so that Job may be saying either 'I could heap up words against you' or, more gently, 'I would make myself a companion to you, condole and sympathise with you in words, and shake my head at you as a mark of fellow-feeling.' He is careful that the gesture here differs from the head-shaking of contempt and derision in Ps. 22:7 and Isa. 37:22. The witnesses do not finally divide; they agree that Job holds up to his comforters the image of their own hardness, and asks them to feel, by exchange of places, the weight of the words they have been so free to heap on him.
5:
Against the cruelty he has just imagined, Job sets the tenderness he would himself have shown, that he would strengthen them with his mouth and let the moving of his lips assuage their grief. The reformed John Gill reads it as the true office of a comforter, which Job had once discharged toward others and would again were his circumstances changed. He would comfort them with the words of his mouth, as God strengthens his people with strength in their souls when he answers them with good and comfortable words, as an angel strengthened Christ in his agony by suggesting comfortable things, and as one saint may strengthen another in distress; and this, Gill notes, is the very thing Eliphaz himself had owned that Job had formerly done for the fainting and the feeble in ch. 4:3-4.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the verse into a lesson on the duty we owe our brethren in affliction. We should say and do all we can to strengthen them, suggesting such considerations as may encourage their confidence in God and support their sinking spirits; for faith and patience are the strength of the afflicted, and whatever helps these graces confirms the feeble knees. And we should labour to assuage their grief, or at least their resentment of its causes. Good words, Henry says, cost nothing, yet they may be of real service to those in sorrow, both as it comforts the sufferer to see his friends concerned for him and as kind words may remind him of what, through the prevalence of grief, he had forgotten; for though hard words break no bones, kind words may help to make broken bones rejoice, and those have the tongue of the learned who know how to speak a word in season to the weary.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke records a bolder rendering that reverses the sense, that of Mr. Good, 'with my own mouth will I overpower you, till the quivering of my lips shall fail,' a version he says is countenanced by the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic. But the received reading, which the other witnesses keep, makes the verse the very opposite of the friends' practice: where they had multiplied words to wound, Job protests he would have multiplied them to heal. The contrast is the point on which all converge — that Job knew, and had once practised, the comforter's art his friends had so wholly failed of, and that the measure of their unkindness is exactly the tenderness he here promises he would have shown in their place. It is the sharpest rebuke of all, delivered not by accusation but by holding up the gentleness they lacked.
6:
'Though I speak, my grief is not assuaged: and though I forbear, what am I eased?' — with this the reply turns from the friends to Job's own strait, and the witnesses feel the closing of every door. The reformed John Gill takes both clauses inwardly: though Job speak to God in prayer, entreating some abatement of his sorrows, he gets no relief; and though he speak to himself in soliloquy, his sorrow is not repressed nor lessened, for he cannot administer to himself the comfort he could once give others were his own case changed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it of the uselessness of reply, 'reprehensions of your conduct will not serve to mitigate my sufferings,' and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the whole simply, 'I cannot but reply, though to reply gives me no relief.'

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry opens here the long and doleful representation of Job's grievances that runs through the following verses, and finds him at a stand whether to smother his complaint or give it vent, since he can find help by neither. Sometimes, Henry says, giving vent to grief gives ease; but though Job speaks, his grief is not assuaged, nay, what he speaks is so misconstrued as to be turned to the aggravation of his grief. At other times keeping silence makes trouble the easier; but though he forbear, he is never the nearer. If he complained, he was censured as passionate; if he was silent, as sullen; if he maintained his integrity, that was his crime; if he made no answer to their accusations, his silence was taken for confession of his guilt. Every way is stopped against him, so that speech and silence are alike unavailing.

Henry draws the sober improvement of it, that we have reason to bless God we are not making such complaints, and that even good men, when in great and extraordinary troubles, have much ado not to entertain hard thoughts of God. The verse is the hinge of the chapter, where the rebuke of miserable comforters gives way to the raw account of a suffering that no words can lighten and no silence can hide; and the witnesses agree in reading it not as petulance but as the honest confession of a man hemmed in on every side, for whom the one relief left is to pour out his tears before God. It is the language of exhaustion, but not yet of despair, for the same lips that own that speaking gives no ease will presently name a witness in heaven who hears.
7:
From the general strait Job passes to its particulars, and the first is a wearied and emptied life: 'he hath made me weary; thou hast made desolate all my company.' The reformed John Gill hears in the opening either 'my grief hath made me weary' or, better, God, whose afflicting hand had made Job weary of the world and of life itself, his troubles heavier than the sand of the sea and his strength unequal to them, so that he could scarcely drag his life along under the weight. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the turn of address that will run through the passage, for here, they note, Job speaks now in the third person of God and now directly to him: 'thou hast made desolate all my company,' by destroying his children and servants and alienating the hearts of his friends.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the desolation into a single weariness — weary of speaking, weary of forbearing, weary of his friends, weary of life itself, his journey through the world grown so uncomfortable that he is quite tired of it. What made it so tiresome, Henry says, was that all his company was made desolate: his children and servants killed, the poor remains of his great household dispersed, and even the company of good people that used to meet at his house for worship now scattered, so that he spent his sabbaths in silence and solitude. He had company indeed, but such as he would rather have been without, for they seemed to triumph in his desolation; and if lovers and friends are put far from us, Henry adds, we must see and own God's hand in it, making our company desolate.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke feels the same double loss and records the Vulgate's turn, 'now my grief oppresses me, and all my joints are reduced to nothing,' but prefers to read Job's own afflictions and the ruin of his family: thou hast made me weary with continual affliction, my strength quite exhausted, and made desolate all my company, not leaving me a single child to continue my name or comfort me in sickness and old age. He notes too Mr. Good's rendering, 'thou hast struck apart all my witnesses.' John Wesley, another wesleyan-arminian voice, keeps the sense plain: it is God who has made him weary, weary of complaining and of life alike, and turned his society into desolation by destroying his children and his servants. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job traces even this stripping of his household to the hand of God, and that the loneliness of a man whose company is gone is itself a heavy article in the account of his grief.
8:
The wasting of Job's body becomes, in this verse, a witness turned against him: 'thou hast filled me with wrinkles, which is a witness against me.' The reformed John Gill is careful that these wrinkles came not through age but through affliction, which had sunk his flesh and furrowed him and made him look far older than his years; yet he adds that this is spoken of the body only, for as to Job's soul, that through the grace of God and the righteousness of his Redeemer was without spot or wrinkle or any such thing. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the rare verb, which occurs only once beside at ch. 22:16 and carries the primary sense of binding and grasping firmly, whence the branch-meanings of comprehending and of wrinkling; the reference to Job's emaciation, and the lines drawn from the picture of one sick with elephantiasis, show that the poet has this shrivelling of the skin in mind.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the same diagnosis: if Job's disease were the elephantiasis, in which the whole skin is wrinkled like the elephant's hide from which the leprosy takes its name, the words would apply most exactly. He owns the obscurity of the verse and gathers the various renderings — Houbigant's, 'my trouble hath weakened all my frame and brought wrinkles over me,' and Mr. Good's, which turns the second clause to an accuser who riseth up and telleth lies to Job's face — but the plain sense stands, that Job's own ravaged body was being read as evidence against him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott names precisely how that reading worked: the wrinkles, like the witness of ch. 10:17, were a witness against him, and certainly in the eyes of his friends they furnished what looked like unquestionable proof of his guilt. This is the bitter irony the witnesses share: the very marks of his suffering, which should have moved compassion, were taken by his comforters as the visible seal of the wickedness they charged him with, so that his affliction was made to argue his sin. His leanness, risen up in him, bore witness to his face — and the friends, mistaking the effect of God's chastening for the badge of a hypocrite, let the sufferer's wasted frame speak against him instead of for him. So Job's body, worn to skin and bone, becomes a false witness in a court where the evidence has been read backward.
9:
'He teareth me in his wrath, who hateth me; he gnasheth upon me with his teeth; mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me' — and over the identity of this tearing enemy the witnesses genuinely divide. The reformed John Gill sets aside both Satan and Eliphaz and takes the enemy to be God himself, of whom Job now had a mistaken apprehension, treating him as his adversary because he thought himself treated as one hated; yet Gill insists this is only Job's darkened notion, for God hates none of his creatures, and though he hates sin and the workers of iniquity, he did not hate his suffering servant. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take a different view, referring the tearing and gnashing not to God and not to the friends but to the men around Job who had envied his prosperity and now rejoiced at his fall, to whom his uprightness had been a burden and who now count themselves rid of their over-righteous liege lord.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke offers yet a third reading, and a striking one: that God permitted Satan to show himself to Job in some horrible form, so that 'he gnasheth upon me with his teeth, mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me' and the verses that follow describe the tempter and his demons, all their host let loose to torture him. Clarke argues that if the words are referred only to the three friends the figures are strained to an insufferable height. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, on the other hand, feels the language almost exceeds even Job's earlier boldness, for here he seems to call God his adversary; and it is hardly possible, Ellicott says, not to understand the expression of God, since Job immediately afterward speaks openly of God. John Wesley touches only the last clause, taking the sharpened eyes as the fierce and sparkling look of one enraged.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, unwilling to force the verse, canvasses all three and lets each stand: it may be Eliphaz, whose words tore Job's good name and thundered terror at him; or Satan, his hater, who by divine permission may have terrified him with apparitions as he later assailed the Saviour in the garden; or God himself, though of him the expressions are as rash as any Job used, for God hates none of his creatures, and it was only Job's melancholy that thus represented to him the terrors of the Almighty. And nothing, Henry adds, can be more grievous to a good man than to apprehend God to be his enemy. So the debate is real and unresolved among the witnesses — whether the enemy who tears is God as Job's clouded grief conceived him, Satan let loose in visible terror, or the envious and scornful men about him — and its very openness measures how far affliction had darkened the sufferer's sense of the God he still, at bottom, trusted.
10:
The tearing of the unseen enemy is matched by the open scorn of men: 'they have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me.' The reformed John Gill reads these as the instruments God suffered to use Job ill, chiefly his friends, who came with open mouth against him, loading him with calumnies and treating him with contempt; and he hears in the gaping mouth the language of Ps. 22:13, 'they gaped upon me as a ravening and a roaring lion,' so that Job here becomes a type of Christ, on whom the reproaches of them that reproached God fell, who was smitten and mocked and scoffed at, and against whom the people cried, 'Crucify him.' The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch are careful that Job does not here mean the three friends but the men around him who envied his prosperity and now rejoice at his misfortune, and they note the construction, that Job says his adversaries make an opening with their mouth and smite his cheeks in contempt and conspire together against him.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the gaping mouths of Job's friends, opened wide against him, and joins the reformed voice in seeing throughout this a foreshadowing of the Passion, for these very expressions are used in the predictions of Christ's sufferings, 'they gaped upon me with their mouths' in Ps. 22:13, and 'they shall smite the judge of Israel upon the cheek' in Mic. 5:1.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the abuse into a picture of general assault: all about him came upon him with open mouth as if they would swallow him alive, offered him every indignity they could invent, and even smote him on the cheek, and in this many were confederate, gathering themselves together against him, even the abjects, as in Ps. 35:15. Herein, Henry says with the ancients, Job was a type of Christ, for the smiting on the cheek with a rod was literally fulfilled when they smote the face of Jesus in Matt. 26:67; and he cries with the psalmist, how were those increased that troubled him. The witnesses differ only over who the mockers are — the friends, for Gill and Wesley, or the envious crowd about him, for Keil and Delitzsch — but they agree that Job feels himself set upon by a whole confederacy of scorn, and that his usage prefigures the derision heaped upon a greater Sufferer, smitten on the cheek and surrounded by open mouths.
11:
Behind every human tormentor Job sees the hand that loosed them: 'God hath delivered me to the ungodly, and turned me over into the hands of the wicked.' The reformed John Gill notes that 'the ungodly' stands in the singular, the evil one, and canvasses whom it may name — Satan, into whose hands God had delivered Job's substance and person, his life excepted, though Job as yet knew nothing of that; or Eliphaz and the friends, whom in his turn he calls evil men for their usage of him; or the Sabeans and Chaldeans, who had been suffered to plunder him. Gill dwells too on the word's force, that it may mean 'God hath shut me up' or 'delivered me bound,' which was literally true of Christ, bound by the Jews and delivered first to the high priest and then to the Roman governor. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is more definite, taking 'the ungodly and the wicked' as the very terms Job now retorts upon his friends, who, he says, have certainly earned them by their conduct.

The witnesses thus divide over the immediate agents. Some look past the friends to Satan or to the raiding nations as the ungodly into whose power Job was given, while Ellicott hears Job flinging the friends' own favourite words back in their faces, so that the men who called him wicked are themselves the wicked he has been handed over to. The difference is real, but it turns on identifying the instrument, not the hand behind it, for on that the voices are wholly at one.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley, with the reformed voice, presses the deeper application: as God delivered Job into wicked hands by his own determinate counsel, so Christ too was delivered into wicked hands, and by the determinate counsel of God, as Peter preached in Acts 2:23. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply carry the picture forward into the verses of assault that follow, where God, having handed Job over, is himself portrayed as breaking and shaking and piercing him. What none of the witnesses doubts is that Job looks beyond the ungodly to the God who gave them their commission, much as David did when Shimei cursed him, owning that they could have had no power against him unless it had been given from above. It is the hardest article of his complaint — not that wicked men afflict him, but that a righteous God has delivered him to them — and it is precisely here, the witnesses observe, that Job most nearly and most mysteriously prefigures the innocent Sufferer given over by the counsel of heaven into the hands of the wicked.
12:
Job remembers the suddenness of his overthrow, the peace that was shattered without warning: 'I was at ease, but he hath broken me asunder.' The reformed John Gill fills in the ease Job had lost — he had been in easy and affluent circumstances, quiet in his nest where he thought to die, and easy too in his mind, a good man enjoying the presence of God and the light of his countenance — and then he was broken to pieces, stripped of his substance, bereft of his children, his body broken with boils and his spirit broken with a sense of divine displeasure, the arrows of God's wrath sticking fast in him. Gill records Broughton's turn, 'I was wealthy, and he hath undone me,' and hears in it the antitype, the Redeemer who, though rich, became poor. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the violence in the very verbs: the intensive form means to crush and crumble in pieces, and the next, to dash in pieces, so that God, taking Job by the neck, raised him on high only to dash him down, and set him up as a mark.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls it a highly poetical passage in which Job becomes, as it were, a St. Sebastian for the arrows of God, and owns it hardly possible to conceive a more vivid picture of his desolate condition under the persecuting hand of the Almighty. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley sharpens the two images: God took him by the neck and shook him as a strong man shakes some stripling he wrestles with, and set him up for a mark that he might shoot all his arrows into him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs how God's dealing seemed to Job, and marks the three hard thoughts it bred, though he will not let them pass uncorrected. It seemed as if God were furious, taking him by the neck as a man in a passion takes a child and shaking him to pieces; and as if he were partial, distinguishing Job from the rest of mankind and setting him up for the butt at which he was pleased to let fly all his arrows, so that they came not by chance but were levelled at him; and yet, Henry adds, whoever our enemies are, we must look on them as God's archers and see him directing the arrow, and say with resignation, it is the Lord, let him do what seemeth him good. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the cry of a man torn from settled peace into sudden ruin, who feels himself singled out as heaven's target, and who must struggle, even while he says it, not to think his God become cruel.
13:
The figure of the marksman widens into a siege of arrows: 'his archers compass me round about, he cleaveth my reins asunder, and doth not spare; he poureth out my gall upon the ground.' The reformed John Gill lets the archers be many things at once — Satan and his powers casting their fiery darts, or the friends shooting their bitter words, or the diseases of Job's body, so many arrows shot into every part of him, besides the arrows of the Almighty and that painful sense of divine wrath. Here too, Gill says, Job is the type: as the archers sorely grieved Joseph and shot at him, so Satan and the scribes and priests surrounded Christ on the cross and shot their blasphemies at him, while justice smote him and the law cast its curse. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the assault to its height, joining this verse to the breach upon breach that follows, and note that God, having handed Job over, is depicted as cleaving his reins without pity and pouring his gall on the ground.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns to the Hebrew and the imagery. The word he renders 'his great ones,' rabbaiv, though the Vulgate and Septuagint make it his spears and the Syriac, Arabic, and Chaldee his arrows; and, following Heath, he finds the whole picture drawn from the huntsman's craft — first the beast is surrounded, then shot dead, then its entrails taken out and its body broken up limb by limb, exactly the sequence Job feels worked upon himself. John Wesley draws the lesson of the archers plainly: whoever our enemies are, we must look upon them as God's archers, and see him directing the arrow.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same cruelty and will not soften it: God seemed to Job to contrive to touch him in the tenderest part, cleaving his reins asunder with acute pains, perhaps the pains of the stone in the region of the kidneys; and as if he kept no mercy in reserve, he does not spare nor abate anything of the extremity, but pours out Job's gall upon the ground as men, having killed a wild beast, open it and pour out the gall with loathing, so that Job thought his very blood counted not precious but nauseous. Even good men, Henry adds, when in great and extraordinary troubles, have much ado not to entertain hard thoughts of God. The witnesses do not divide over the terror of the picture; they weigh only who the archers are — demons, friends, diseases, or the arrows of God himself — and agree that Job feels himself hunted, surrounded, and struck through, a quarry brought down and opened by a hand that will not spare.
14:
The relentlessness of the assault is caught in a single military image: 'he breaketh me with breach upon breach, he runneth upon me like a giant.' The reformed John Gill reads the breaches as the blows that came thick and fast upon Job's substance, his family, and the health of his body, one hard upon another, and hears behind them the report of those first messengers of evil tidings, when, as the earlier narrative told, while one was yet speaking another came with worse. The affliction, on his reading, is a wall stormed again and again, each fresh assault opening a new gap before the last was mended.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the same figure of a besieged fortress, joining the verse to the pouring-out of gall that precedes it, and render the second clause of God running upon Job like a mighty warrior, a hero charging a foe too weak to stand. The picture, on their reading, is of a strong man bearing down with irresistible force on one who has no power to resist, so that the very disproportion of the combat is part of Job's complaint.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out both halves. God seemed to Job unreasonable and insatiable in his executions, following him with one wound after another: so his troubles came at first, while one messenger was speaking another arrived, and so it was still, new boils rising every day, so that he had no prospect of the end of his sufferings. And God seemed to run upon him like a giant, whom he could not possibly stand before or confront, as the giants of old ran down all their poor neighbours and were too hard for them. Yet Henry, here as throughout, marks that this is how the affliction appeared to a mind darkened by grief, and adds the caution that even good men, under great and extraordinary troubles, have much ado not to entertain hard thoughts of God. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse measures not the malice of God but the ceaselessness of the suffering, a man stormed like a city whose walls are breached faster than he can repair them, and charged by an adversary of such overwhelming strength that resistance never enters his thought. It is the language of one utterly overborne, who feels the blows come without pause and without proportion, and who can only name the force that overwhelms him and confess that he cannot withstand it.
15:
Under such blows Job describes how low he has stooped: 'I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and defiled my horn in the dust.' The reformed John Gill supposes he put on this coarse mourning when he rent his mantle and sat in ashes, and notes that some read the word for skin as the thin skin newly drawn over a wound, so that the rough cloth pressed on tender flesh; and he weighs whether Job was so reduced as to have no better clothing, though he thinks rather this was the voluntary humiliation of a mourner. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch observe that Job does not merely put the sackcloth on but sews it upon his naked body, and attribute this to the hideous distortion of the frame by elephantiasis, which would not admit the ordinary form of clothes; the same disease is why he speaks not of his skin simply but of its scurfy, scaly surface.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke dwells on the defiled horn, the emblem of power and eminence taken from the horned beasts, worn on ancient crowns and helmets and still, he reports from Bruce's travels, an ornament on the foreheads of the chiefs of Abyssinia, a conical piece of gilded silver called the kirn, worn after victory, which explains the many scriptural charges not to lift up the horn on high. To defile or roll the horn in the dust, Clarke concludes, signifies the disgrace and destruction of power and authority; and he rejects Mr. Good's turn, 'I have rolled my turban in the dust,' as mistaking the Hebrew.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, keeping the second clause figurative, would read the first the same way, taking the sewn sackcloth to speak of Job's skin itself, grown hard and rugged as haircloth under the disease. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole as the deliberate self-abasement of one truly penitent and truly patient, humbling himself under the mighty hand of God: he laid aside his ornaments and soft clothing, thinking silk unsuitable upon such sores, and sewed the sackcloth on as resolved to continue his humiliation as long as his affliction lasted; and he insisted on no points of honour, but laid his horn in the dust, refusing the respect once paid his dignity, for when God brings down our condition that should bring down our spirits, and it is better to lay the horn in the dust than to lift it up against Providence and have it broken at last. Against Eliphaz, who had painted Job as high and unhumbled, Henry hears him answer, 'no, the dust is now the fittest place for me.' The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse shows a man not proudly resisting his stroke but sinking under it in penitent grief, his glory laid low in the dust of his own accord.
16:
'My face is foul with weeping, and on my eyelids is the shadow of death' — the outward tokens of a grief wept almost to blindness. The reformed John Gill notes that the word carries in the Arabic the sense of redness, even of fermenting red wine, and so aptly describes a face grown red and swollen and blubbered with excessive weeping; and he names the causes of those tears — the loss of his substance and his children, the unkindness of his friends, the corruptions he felt working in him, and above all the hiding of God's face. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the rare intensive form, which means not that the eyes are kindled but that they are reddened all over from weeping, and so weakened that the shadow of death, the deep gloom named already at ch. 10:21, seems to settle on his eyelids; his eyes are sad even to the darkness of the grave.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the verse a man who has banished mirth as unseasonable and set himself to sow in tears, his face foul with weeping so constant for his sins, for God's displeasure, and for his friends' unkindness, that it has brought a shadow of death upon his eyelids; he had not only wept away his beauty but almost wept his eyes out. And in this, Henry adds, Job was again a type of Christ, who was a man of sorrows, much in tears, and who pronounced those blessed that mourn, for they shall be comforted.

The witnesses do not divide; and the sober weight of the verse lies in what Keil and Delitzsch draw from its place, that this exceedingly miserable state and appearance belong to a man who is nevertheless no disguised hypocrite needing to do penance in sackcloth, but an innocent sufferer, as the next verse will avow. The redness of the wept-out eyes, the death-shadow on the lids, are not the marks of a guilt found out but of a sorrow poured toward God; for Job weeps, Henry says, not with the sorrow of the world but after a godly sort, before the Lord. So the verse gathers the whole picture of his wasted body and abased estate into the single image of a face ruined by tears, and sets it, deliberately, on the very threshold of his great protestation of innocence, that the reader may see the sufferer plainly before he hears him swear his hands are clean. The mourning is real, the grief unfeigned, and yet it is the mourning of a clear conscience, which is why it can rise, in the verses to come, from the dust of weeping to a witness in heaven.
17:
At the depth of his abasement Job turns the whole complaint upon its hinge, protesting that all this has come 'not for any injustice in mine hands: also my prayer is pure.' The reformed John Gill is careful to say what Job does and does not claim: not that there was no sin in his heart or life, for he had owned such infirmities already, but that there was nothing in his hands got by unjust means, no man's property taken, no justice perverted as a magistrate by bribes or the accepting of persons, and he could challenge any to prove otherwise, as Samuel once did before Israel. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears him assert it with his last breath, that the charges of his friends are groundless, that he is afflicted unto death but not for his iniquities, and that his prayer is pure — 'I am no hypocrite, God knoweth.' John Wesley joins the two clauses: all this has not come for any injurious dealing, but for reasons known to God only, and Job does not cast off God's fear and service, as Eliphaz had charged at ch. 15:4, but still prays with a sincere heart.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the Hebrew, that it is literally 'for no injustice,' just as Isa. 53:9 is rightly read 'not because he had done any violence, or because deceit was in his mouth' — the innocent Servant and the innocent sufferer sharing the same acquittal. Keil and Delitzsch keep the clause as the ground of the appeal that follows, the claim of clean hands and pure prayer being the warrant on which Job dares to call earth and heaven to witness.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers it as the great support that held Job up amid all his griefs, the testimony of a conscience void of offence. Toward men he could say, 'not for any injustice in my hands,' for he had always despised the gain of oppression, whatever Eliphaz alleged; and toward God, 'my prayer is pure,' for prayer cannot be pure while there is injustice in the hands, as Isaiah warns at Isa. 1:15, yet Job's, though not free from all infirmity, was free from reigning and allowed guile, not like the prayers of those who look no further than to be seen of men. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that this verse is the turning-point of the chapter, where the sufferer, having described his ruin, plants his feet on his integrity, and that the cleanness of his hands and the purity of his prayer are precisely what embolden him, in the next breath, to summon the earth and heaven as witnesses to his cause.
18:
'O earth, cover not thou my blood, and let my cry have no place' — the cry of a man who will not let his cause be buried, and the witnesses divide over its very drift. The reformed John Gill takes it as an imprecation upon himself: if Job had been guilty of any capital crime, of blood or oppression, let the earth never cover or conceal it, but disclose it and spread it abroad, that all might know and he suffer shame, even as the earth is said to disclose the blood of the slain when inquisition is made for it. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way, that the earth covers the blood which lies undiscovered and unrevenged, so Job says, if I be guilty of destroying any man, let the earth disclose it, and let the cry of my complaints or prayers find no place in the ears of God or men if this be true.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke prefers the opposite sense, hearing a clear allusion to the murder of Abel and reading it as Job's call for justice against his own destroyers: his blood is his life, taken from him by violence, and he prays it may cry against those who slay him as Abel's blood cried against Cain from the ground in Gen. 4:10. Clarke weighs the other view, that Job, conscious of innocence, bids the earth not cover any blood shed by him, but judges it unsupported by the Hebrew and unknown to the ancient versions.

The grammatical-historical voices attend to the second clause. Charles Ellicott renders 'let my cry have no place' as 'let there be no place in the wide earth where my cry shall not reach; let it have no resting-place, but fill the whole earth' — a cry that will not be quieted till it is answered. Keil and Delitzsch set the verse against the old idea that unavenged blood lies bare, uncovered, till vengeance find it, as in Ezek. 24:7 and Isa. 26:21, so that Job, in the consciousness of his innocence, calls on the earth not to suck in his blood as of one guilty, but to leave it exposed until it be avenged. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds both senses together: if any blood-guilt were on Job, let it not be concealed, for murder will out and the earth shall one day disclose her blood, as in Isa. 26:21; but he adds a further and probable sense, that Job here lays his death upon the friends whose harsh censures broke his heart, charging the guilt of his blood upon them and begging that his cry might have no place to lie hid, but come up to heaven and be heard by him that makes inquisition for blood. The witnesses do not resolve the ambiguity; they leave the verse trembling between a plea for the disclosure of guilt, if any there be, and a demand that innocent blood cry aloud and unresting until God avenge it.
19:
Out of the cry that will not rest, Job lifts his eyes above the earth: 'also now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and my record is on high.' The reformed John Gill reads the witness as God himself, who dwells in the heavens and beholds all the sons of men, the all-seeing Being to whom Job appeals — that if he be guilty God may witness against him, but if innocent, that God may witness for him, as Job believes he will. The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the appeal to God: Adam Clarke hears simply, 'I appeal to God for my innocence,' and John Wesley adds that besides the witness of his own conscience, God is witness of his integrity. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the parallel lines, 'in heaven is my Witness, and One who acknowledgeth me is in the heights,' setting them within the great turn where Job, mocked by his friends, appeals from earth to the God on high who knows his cause.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the wonder of the confession and marks its bearing on the famous words of chapter 19. What, he asks, can the believer in the full light of the Gospel say more, who knows of One in heaven ever making intercession for him? and yet Job's faith had already risen to such a height and grasped such a hope; in no other book of the Bible, he says, is there such a picture of faith clinging to the all-just God for justification. Here Ellicott's language hovers on the edge of a deeper reading, for the 'One in heaven' who witnesses and acknowledges begins to look like more than the Judge himself.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes explicit the comfort in it: the witness in our own bosom will stand us in little stead unless we have a witness in heaven too, for God is greater than our hearts and we are not to be our own judges; and it is an unspeakable comfort to a good man, lying under the censure of his brethren, that there is a God in heaven who knows his integrity and will clear it up, this one witness being instead of a thousand, as the Lord's own witness to the Son is urged in John 5:37. The witnesses here stand together in taking the witness for God himself, the searcher who knows Job's cause; yet the question that will divide them opens already in this verse — whether that heavenly witness and advocate is simply God appealed to against God, or, as the gospel sense will press at v.21, a distinct Mediator on high who pleads a man's cause with God. For now the confession stands in its own strength: whatever men on earth may say, Job's record is written and his witness enthroned where no slander can reach.
20:
'My friends scorn me: but mine eye poureth out tears unto God' — and the verse sets the coldness of earth against the appeal to heaven. The reformed John Gill is careful about what the scorn touches: not that the friends mocked Job's afflictions and diseases, which would have been brutish, but that they scorned his words, the arguments and reasons he brought in his own defence. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the contrast sharp: 'they deride and insult me, but my eye is toward God; I look to him to vindicate my cause.'

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would render the opening as an apostrophe, 'ye my scorners, who profess and ought to be my friends,' and then let the tears run straight into the plea of the following verse: mine eye poureth out tears unto God that he would maintain the right of man with God, and of the son of man with his neighbour; or, that one might plead for man with God as the son of man pleadeth for his neighbour — the very thing, he notes, that Job had already longed for at ch. 9:33, where he wished for a daysman to lay his hand upon them both. On Ellicott's reading the verse does not merely lament the friends' scorn but turns it at once into prayer, the mockery of men becoming the occasion of the eye's appeal to heaven.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs both halves as the case between Job and his friends and the case between Job and God. Toward the friends he stood helpless, for they were of counsel against him and used all their art and eloquence to run him down, and the scorns of friends, Henry observes, are more cutting than those of enemies, though we must expect them and provide accordingly. But toward God his tears found their channel: he had said before that he wept much, and here he tells us which way his tears ran, poured out to God; his sorrow was not that of the world, but he sorrowed after a godly sort, wept before the Lord, and offered the sacrifice of a broken heart. Even tears, Henry adds, when sanctified to God, give ease to troubled spirits, and if men slight our grief, this may comfort us, that God regards it. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse turns on that single 'but' — scorned by the friends who should have wept with him, Job weeps instead before the God who alone will hear, and his tears become not the overflow of despair but a mute pleading directed upward, the eye doing the work the tongue can no longer do among men.
21:
The tears of the eye become a formed petition, that God would grant a hearing such as men allow one another: 'O that one might plead for a man with God, as a man pleadeth for his neighbour.' The reformed John Gill reads the wish plainly, that one might be appointed and allowed to plead with God on Job's behalf, or that Job himself be admitted to plead his own cause, and that God would decide the matter in controversy between him and his friends, which Job doubts not would be given on his side. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set it among the terms of the trial Job longs for, the cry of a man who wants his case brought before God and adjudged; and Charles Ellicott ties it back to the daysman Job had already sighed for at ch. 9:33, the umpire who might lay his hand upon both parties, so that here the same longing returns, that one might plead for man with God as the son of man pleads for his neighbour.

Yet just here the witnesses open a real division over how far the verse reaches. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the two readings side by side. On the one hand the words may be simply Job's wish for such freedom at God's bar as men have at the bar of a magistrate, confident that with the Judge himself a witness to his integrity he would carry his cause, in the spirit of Isa. 50:8, 'he is near that justifieth me.' But Henry adds that some give a gospel sense of the verse, which the original will well bear: 'he will plead,' that is, there is one that will plead for man with God, even the Son of man for his friend; and those who pour out their tears before God, unable to plead for themselves by reason of their distance and defects, have a Friend to plead for them, even the Son of man, on whom we must bottom all our hope of acceptance with God.

So the debate the earlier verse only hinted at now stands open: whether Job merely craves a fair hearing before God, God being at once his witness and his judge, or whether the yearning after 'one to plead for a man with God' reaches, however dimly, toward a distinct Mediator, the Son of man who pleads his people's cause on high. Gill and Ellicott keep the wish within the horizon of Job's own longing for an umpire; Henry allows both, and finds in the gospel sense the answer that Job's darkness was groping after. The witnesses do not force the text either way; they leave it as one of those places where an Old Testament sufferer's cry for an advocate seems to strain beyond itself, and where the reader who knows the Son of man cannot but hear more than Job himself could yet have understood.
22:
The appeal for a hearing is pressed by the shortness of the time left: 'when a few years are come, then I shall go the way whence I shall not return.' The reformed John Gill notes that man's years are few at best, and Job's remaining fewer still in his own apprehension; the phrase is literally 'years of number,' years that God has fixed and determined, or that, being few, are easily counted. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke prefers Mr. Good's version, 'but the years numbered to me are come, and I must go the way whence I shall not return,' for Job could look for no long life but expected death every hour, feeling himself already in the arms of death and seeing the grave as good as dug to receive him. John Wesley reads 'go' as departing to the state and place of the dead, whence men cannot return to this life; his death hastens, and therefore he earnestly desires that the cause depending between him and his friends may be determined, that if guilty he may bear the shame before all men, and if innocent, that his integrity and the credit of religion may be vindicated.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the same phrase, 'years of number,' meaning either years easily numbered, as 'men of number' in Gen. 34:20 means few men, or years that are allotted and determined. It is strange, he grants, to find Job in his condition speaking of years at all, as strange as to find a man so tormented sustaining so long an argument; and he offers, as no more than a suggestion, that the narrative may be an ideal setting forth the low estate of sin-stricken humanity, or else that Job speaks in contemplation of himself simply as a dying man.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the verse into a meditation on death as the crown of a good man's integrity. To die is to go the way whence we shall not return, to set out on a long journey for good and all, removing from this world to another, from the world of sense to the world of spirits, to our long home, with no coming back to our state here nor any change of our state there. We must all, Henry says, very certainly and very shortly go this journey; and it is comfortable to those who keep a good conscience to think of it, for such confidence had Job toward God that he could take pleasure in the approach of death, when he should be determined to his everlasting state as one who doubted not it would then be well with him. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job urges the nearness of his end as a reason for a speedy hearing, that the traveller already at the edge of the road that has no return may have his cause tried while there is yet a little time. And they leave the chapter where his faith has quietly brought it — a dying man, scorned by his friends and broken by his God, who nevertheless commits his integrity to a witness in heaven and goes toward the grave not as one without hope but as one whose everlasting state is safe.
